# SQL and Python Integration

:::cdi-message
- **ID:** DBSQL-F-L06
- **Type:** Lesson
- **Audience:** Public
- **Theme:** Query then analyze
:::

SQL and Python work best together when responsibilities are clear.

- SQL shapes data through relational logic
- Python extends analysis, visualization, and modeling

SQLite engine behavior is documented in the official documentation @sqliteDocs.

---

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: l06-setup
#| include: false

import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

con = sqlite3.connect("data/cdi-retail.sqlite")
```

---

## Revenue per Customer

```{python}
#| label: l06-revenue-per-customer
#| echo: true

query = '''
SELECT c.full_name,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
GROUP BY c.full_name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
'''

df = pd.read_sql(query, con)
print(df)
```

---

## Visualize the Summary

```{python}
#| label: l06-revenue-bar
#| echo: true

plt.bar(df["full_name"], df["revenue"])
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.title("Revenue by Customer")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

---

## Why SQL First Matters

A common workflow mistake is to load full tables into Python and then join or filter there.

Better practice is to:

- Filter in SQL
- Join in SQL
- Aggregate in SQL
- Transfer only structured results into Python

This keeps analysis efficient and reduces opportunities for structural mistakes.
